blocks.text: K. stared at the inspector. He was getting schoolmasterly lessons here from someone perhaps younger than himself? For his candor he was punished with a rebuke? And about the reason for his arrest and those who had ordered it he learned nothing?

He fell into a certain agitation, walked up and down, which no one prevented him from doing, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair into place, passed by the three gentlemen, said, "It makes no sense at all," whereupon they turned toward him and looked at him obligingly, yet gravely, and finally came to a halt once more before the inspector's table. "Public Prosecutor Hasterer is a good friend of mine," he said, "may I telephone him?" "Certainly," said the inspector, "though I do not know what sense there would be in that, unless you have some private matter of your own to discuss with him." "What sense?" cried K., more dismayed than annoyed. "Who are you, anyway? You ask for sense and are staging the most senseless thing there is. Is it not enough to move a stone to pity? First these gentlemen ambushed me, and now they sit or stand about here and make me go through my paces before you. What sense there would be in telephoning a public prosecutor when I am supposedly under arrest? Very well, I shall not telephone." "Why, by all means," said the inspector, stretching out his hand toward the anteroom, where the telephone was, "please do telephone." "No, I no longer wish to," said K., and went to the window. Across the way the party was still at the window, and seemed only now, because K. had stepped up to the window, a little disturbed in the quiet of their watching. The old couple made to rise, but the man behind them calmed them. "There are spectators of the same sort over there," K. called out quite loudly to the inspector, pointing outside with his forefinger. "Away from there," he then shouted across. The three promptly drew back a few steps at once, the two old people even retreating behind the man, who shielded them with his broad body and, to judge by the movements of his mouth, was saying something unintelligible at that distance. Yet they did not vanish altogether, but seemed to be waiting for the moment when they might approach the window again unnoticed. "Intrusive, inconsiderate people!" said K. as he turned back into the room. The inspector possibly agreed with him, as K. thought he could discern with a sidelong glance. But it was just as possible that he had not been listening at all, for he had pressed one hand firmly down upon the table and seemed to be comparing the lengths of his fingers. The two warders were sitting on a trunk draped with an ornamental cover and rubbing their knees. The three young men had set their hands on their hips and were looking aimlessly about. It was quiet, as in some forgotten office. "Well, gentlemen," cried K.—for a moment it seemed to him as though he were carrying them all on his shoulders—"to judge by your appearance, my affair would seem to be concluded. I am of the opinion that it is best to reflect no further upon the justification or lack of justification of your proceedings and to bring the matter to an amicable close with a mutual handshake. If you share my opinion, then please"—and he stepped up to the inspector's table and held out his hand to him. The inspector raised his eyes, bit his lips, and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still believed the inspector would take it. The latter, however, stood up, picked up a hard round hat that was lying on Fräulein Bürstner's bed, and placed it carefully on his head with both hands, as one does when trying on new hats. "How simple everything seems to you!" he said to K. as he did so, "we should bring the matter to an amicable close, you thought? No, no, that really will not do. By which, on the other hand, I by no means wish to say that you should despair. No, why should you? You are merely under arrest, nothing further. That was what I had to communicate to you, I have done so, and I have also seen how you received it. With that it is enough for today, and we may take our leave, though only provisionally. You will presumably wish to go to the bank now?" "To the bank?" asked K., "I thought I was under arrest." K. asked with a certain defiance, for although his handshake had not been accepted, he felt himself, especially since the inspector had stood up, growing ever more independent of all these people. He was playing with them. He had the intention, should they leave, of running after them down to the street door and offering them his arrest. For that reason he also repeated: "How can I go to the bank, seeing that I am under arrest?" "Ah, I see," said the inspector, who was already at the door, "you have misunderstood me. You are under arrest, certainly, but that is not meant to prevent you from carrying out your profession. Nor are you to be hindered in your ordinary way of life." "Then being under arrest is not very bad," said K., going up close to the inspector. "I never meant anything else," said the latter. "In that case, however, even the notification of the arrest scarcely seems to have been very necessary," said K., and moved closer still. The others had drawn closer too. All of them were now gathered in a narrow space by the door. "It was my duty," said the inspector. "A stupid duty," said K. unrelentingly. "That may be," replied the inspector, "but let us not waste our time with such talk. I had assumed that you wished to go to the bank. Since you weigh every word, I add: I am not forcing you to go to the bank, I had merely assumed that you wished to. And to make that easier for you, and to render your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I have kept these three gentlemen, your colleagues, at your disposal here." "What?" cried K., staring at the three in astonishment. These utterly nondescript, bloodless young men, whom he still had in his memory only as a group beside the photographs, were indeed clerks from his bank—not colleagues, that was saying too much and was already a gap in the inspector's omniscience, yet subordinate clerks from the bank they certainly were. How could K. have overlooked that? How absorbed he must have been by the inspector and the warders not to recognize these three. The stiff Rabensteiner swinging his hands, the blond Kullich with his deep-set eyes, and Kaminer with the insufferable smile caused by a chronic muscular strain—"Good morning!" said K. after a little while, holding out his hand to the gentlemen as they bowed with proper formality. "I did not recognize you at all. Well then, we shall go to work now, shall we not?" The gentlemen nodded laughingly and eagerly, as though they had been waiting for that the entire time, except that when K. missed his hat, which had been left behind in his room, they all ran off one after another to fetch it, which did after all point to a certain embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them go through the two open doors; the last, naturally, was the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had broken into no more than an elegant trot. Kaminer handed over the hat, and K., as was indeed often necessary at the bank as well, had to remind himself expressly that Kaminer's smile was not intentional, indeed that he could not smile intentionally at all. In the anteroom Frau Grubach, who did not look particularly guilty at all, then opened the door of the flat for the whole party, and K. looked down, as he so often did, at her apron string, which cut so needlessly deep into her massive bulk. Downstairs, watch in hand, K. decided to take a motorcar so as not to prolong needlessly a delay that already amounted to half an hour. Kaminer ran to the corner to summon the car; the other two were obviously trying to distract K., when suddenly Kullich pointed to the doorway of the house opposite, in which the tall man with the blond pointed beard had just appeared and in the first instant, a little embarrassed at now showing himself at his full height, stepped back against the wall and leaned there. The old couple were presumably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for drawing attention to the man whom he himself had already seen earlier, whom indeed he had even been expecting. "Do not look across," he burst out, without noticing how strange such a manner of speaking was toward independent men. Nor was any explanation necessary, however, for just then the motorcar arrived, they took their seats, and drove off. Then K. remembered that he had not noticed the departure of the inspector and the warders at all; the inspector had obscured the three clerks from him, and now in turn the clerks had obscured the inspector. That did not show much presence of mind, and K. resolved to watch himself more closely in this respect. Yet involuntarily he still turned round and leaned forward over the rear deck of the motorcar, on the chance of still catching sight of the inspector and the warders. At once, however, he turned back again and leaned comfortably into the corner of the car without having made so much as an attempt to look for anyone. Although it did not appear so, just now he would have been in need of some encouragement, yet the gentlemen now seemed tired; Rabensteiner looked out of the car to the right, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer remained at his disposal with his grin, about which humanity regrettably forbade making a joke.
